title: Drumheller: Dinosaur Capital of the World
summary: The Alberta badlands town with the world's largest dinosaur statue - where you can climb inside a T. rex's mouth for views of the valley that's produced some of paleontology's most important fossil discoveries.

content.intro: In the Alberta badlands, where the Red Deer River has carved striped canyons through ancient sediments, the town of Drumheller has claimed an audacious title: 'Dinosaur Capital of the World.' The claim has merit. The badlands surrounding Drumheller have produced some of paleontology's most significant dinosaur discoveries, including complete skeletons of Albertosaurus, Gorgosaurus, and dozens of other species. The Royal Tyrrell Museum, just outside town, is one of the world's premier dinosaur museums. And at the town entrance, a 25-meter (82-foot) fiberglass T. rex welcomes visitors - the World's Largest Dinosaur, which you can climb inside and look out through its teeth. Drumheller has committed fully to its prehistoric identity: dinosaur murals, dinosaur trash cans, dinosaur everything. The commitment is justified. These badlands are where dinosaurs come to be found.

sections.title: The Fossils
sections.body: The badlands around Drumheller expose rocks from the Late Cretaceous period, 70-75 million years ago - the end of the age of dinosaurs. The Dinosaur Park Formation and Horseshoe Canyon Formation have produced thousands of specimens. Joseph Tyrrell discovered the first major find in 1884: an Albertosaurus skull. Since then, 40 dinosaur species have been identified from the region, including predators (Albertosaurus, Gorgosaurus), duck-billed dinosaurs (Edmontosaurus, Parasaurolophus), horned dinosaurs (Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus), and armored dinosaurs (Ankylosaurus). The badlands continue to yield new discoveries as erosion exposes fresh fossils each year.

sections.title: The Museum
sections.body: The Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology opened in 1985, named for Joseph Tyrrell. The museum holds over 160,000 specimens and displays nearly 40 complete dinosaur skeletons. Exhibits cover the entire history of life, from Precambrian bacteria to Ice Age mammals, but dinosaurs are the stars. The museum is a working research facility; visitors can watch paleontologists preparing fossils in the laboratory. Outdoor programs take participants into the badlands to search for fossils. The museum draws over 400,000 visitors annually to a town of 8,000 - the most-visited attraction in Alberta outside the Rocky Mountains.

sections.title: The Big Dinosaur
sections.body: The World's Largest Dinosaur is an 25-meter (82-foot) fiberglass T. rex standing at the entrance to Drumheller. Visitors can climb 106 stairs inside the structure and look out through the dinosaur's open mouth - a viewing platform offering badlands vistas. The statue was built in 2000 at a cost of $1.4 million, funded partly by provincial grants and partly by community fundraising. It's not anatomically accurate (the arms are too long, the head too large), but accuracy isn't the point. The World's Largest Dinosaur announces Drumheller's identity and provides an irresistible photo opportunity. It's become one of Canada's most photographed landmarks.

sections.title: The Badlands
sections.body: The Canadian Badlands formed as the Red Deer River and its tributaries carved through soft sedimentary rock, exposing bands of sandstone, mudstone, and coal. The result is a stark landscape of hoodoos (mushroom-shaped rock pillars), coulees (dry valleys), and striped hillsides. The badlands support sparse vegetation and few people - too rough for farming, too dry for ranching. But they're perfect for fossil hunting. Erosion constantly exposes new specimens; paleontologists and amateurs find bones simply by walking. The colors are spectacular: reds, oranges, grays, and blacks layered across the hills. The landscape is simultaneously ancient and constantly changing.

sections.title: Visiting Drumheller
sections.body: Drumheller is located 130 kilometers northeast of Calgary, Alberta, on Highway 9. The Royal Tyrrell Museum is 6 kilometers northwest of town; admission is charged, and timed tickets are recommended in summer. The World's Largest Dinosaur is in downtown Drumheller; admission is charged to climb inside. The Dinosaur Trail, a scenic loop road, passes hoodoos, viewpoints, and the museum. The badlands are accessible year-round, but summer is peak season. Drumheller has hotels, restaurants, and full services. Calgary International Airport is the nearest major hub. Allow at least a full day for the museum and scenic drives; dinosaur enthusiasts will want more.

content.flightContext: Located at 51.47°N, 112.70°W in the Red Deer River valley of Alberta. From altitude, Drumheller appears as a small town in a dramatic badlands landscape - the river valley surrounded by eroded terrain, hoodoos visible as irregular formations. The Royal Tyrrell Museum is visible northwest of town. The terrain is striped badlands, starkly different from the surrounding prairie. Calgary is 130 kilometers southwest. The Dinosaur Provincial Park (another major fossil site) is 150 kilometers southeast. The isolation of the badlands is visible from altitude - few roads, few structures, just eroded rock.
